newsitem.title: DENMARK: Copenhagen ends year as Europe's culture capital.
newsitem.headline: Copenhagen ends year as Europe's culture capital.

text.p: Copenhagen rounded off its year as European Cultural Capital at a ceremony on Saturday, passing on Europe's cultural torch to Salonika, Greece, for the coming year.

"Cultural Capital '96 has extended our entire conception of the city," Copenhagen Mayor Jens Kramer Mikkelsen said in a speech to Salonika's mayor Konstantinos Kosmopoulos and 1,500 other guests. "The year has been a great success, it has completely transformed the city," Trevor Davies, the British director of Copenhagen Cultural Capital '96 told Reuters.
"We have given the old lady a face lift. We have promoted Copenhagen to the first division as a European cultural city," he said.

But the much-trumpeted 12-month, 1.2 billion crown ($200 million), multi-event arts jamboree attended by an estimated 10 million people, received a mixed reception from residents of the Danish capital.

A Gallup survey showed only 22 percent of citizens of greater Copenhagen expressing positive interest in Cultural Capital, with 52 percent confessing to only minimal interest in the city's greatest ever cultural spectacle.
Only five percent actually displayed any great enthusiasm for the project, according to Gallup.

The year's one hundred imported events included exhibitions of paintings by Rembrandt, French impressionists and Picasso, an Islamic exhibition, music festivals with top European orchestras, classical soloists, opera, ballet, theatre, rock, jazz and modern dance.
The most popular single event was a gigantic summer Japanese EDO firework display along Copenhagen's waterfront, which attracted almost a half million spectators.
The title of Cultural Capital rotates annually among European Union cities. The first host was Athens in 1985.
